properties.title: Saga: an in silico ontology for a multimodal patient world model

membership.reason: Saga is a multimodal patient world model with shared latent state S_j, treatment- and time-conditioned stochastic transitions, recursive event feedback, and branching treatment rollouts.
membership.counting_boundary: Verified L3 branching/counterfactual multimodal patient world model (WT_EHR, BP_COMPARE).

properties.backbone: Grouped temporal causal Transformer + treatment/time-conditioned stochastic transition + clinical readout heads + conditional DDIM image generator

properties.flow: Multimodal irregular history H_j -> shared state S_j -> treatment/time-conditioned stochastic rollout S_{j+1} -> events, progression/OS readouts, and DDIM images

properties.purpose: Multimodal oncology disease-course simulation, progression/survival forecasting, and future image synthesis.
properties.environment: 461,370 oncology patients across 112 centres (internal, temporal, geographical external)

evidence_fragments.content: Here we introduce Saga, a multimodal patient world model that learns a shared state from patient histories to predict clinical events and generate multimodal images. Generated events and times are appended to the history and re-encoded to advance prediction. We studied 461,370 patients with 12 cancer types across 112 centres. Modality-specific paired evaluations linked future images to observed follow-up. With historical images held fixed, removing patient conditioning reduced event F1 from 0.716 to 0.591 and increased lesion-burden error from 11.8% to 21.3%. In free rollouts, eight-step event F1 was 0.672, compared with 0.553 for a longitudinal Transformer evaluated from the same origins, and timing error was lower by 8.7 days. In the internal test set, one-year progression AUROC was 0.882, with values of 0.871 and 0.856 in temporal and geographical external evaluations.

Patients are assigned to development and evaluation sets before prediction origins and observation pairs are generated, with all records from each patient retained in the same partition. Geographically external evaluation holds out entire centres. Temporal holdout includes subsequently eligible patients from development centres after a prespecified date cutoff, excluding patients already assigned to development or internal testing. Development uses only training information available before the cutoff. Each task defines origins at eligible encounters and truncates history by information-availability time; treatment inputs include only treatments and plans documented at the origin.

[paraphrase (visual p.5)] Fig. 1 (p. 5): Multimodal longitudinal inputs (US/MR/CT imaging, pathology slides, clinical text, structured events; 461,370 patients, 112 centres, 12 cancers) -> event-token assembly & grouped temporal causal attention longitudinal Transformer -> shared latent patient state S_j = q_phi(H_j) -> treatment- & time-conditioned stochastic transition S_{j+1} ~ p_theta(. | S_j, A_j, delta_j) -> recursive treatment-conditioned rollouts (Treatment A A_j^(A) vs Treatment B A_j^(B)), multimodal clinical readouts, and conditional DDIM future image generation.

locator.section_or_table: Results — Event feedback and free rollout

evidence_fragments.content: In the stepwise comparison, event F1 at 1, 2, 4 and 8 steps was 0.781, 0.754, 0.716 and 0.672 for Saga, compared with 0.751, 0.704, 0.627 and 0.553 for the longitudinal Transformer (Fig. 4a). The absolute F1 difference increased from 0.030 at one step to 0.119 at eight steps. At the eight-step evaluation depth, direct multihorizon prediction and frozen-latent-state controls achieved event F1 values of 0.579 and 0.531. Saga’s timing MAE increased from 9.2 days at one step to 27.4 days at eight steps, remaining below the Transformer’s corresponding errors of 11.8 and 36.1 days, with an eight-step reduction of 8.7 days (Fig. 4b).

[paraphrase (visual p.12)] Fig. 3f (p. 12) patient and treatment conditioning comparisons on matched histories (historical images fixed): Original conditioning (Event-F1 0.716, lesion-burden MAE 11.8%, feature preservation 0.923, progression-risk shift Ref.), No treatment conditioning (0.681, 15.6%, 0.887, +0.071), Alternative treatment token (0.694, 14.8%, 0.901, +0.043). Caption explicitly notes risk shifts do not indicate direction of benefit.
Output differences under alternative treatment conditions describe model responses; causal interpretation requires an appropriate identification design[46].

capability_assessments.rationale: Treatment- and time-conditioned multimodal patient world model with implemented persistent shared latent state S_j (019), learned stochastic temporal transitions (041, 042), evaluated 1-to-8-step recursive rollouts (053), evaluated treatment conditioning (043), and matched-history alternative-treatment comparison in Fig. 3f (039; L3 functional comparison). Authors explicitly note that alternative-treatment shifts reflect conditional model responses rather than causally identified treatment effects (pp. 8, 19).

readiness_assessments.legacy_highest_label: R2 Multi-centre temporal & geographical external validation

limitations: Retrospective multi-centre oncology cohorts; no prospective clinical trial or closed-loop decision deployment.
